title: Not One Stone Left
sum: Jesus leaves the Temple for the last time and tells his disciples that every stone of it will be pulled down. On the Mount of Olives they ask when, and what sign will mark his coming and the end of the age. He warns them against false messiahs, wars and panic, tells those in Judea to flee when they see "the abomination of desolation," and describes great suffering, a darkened sky, and the Son of Man coming on the clouds to gather his chosen.

Then the tone changes. "This generation" will see these things, but no one, not even the Son, knows the day or the hour. Like the people of Noah's day, many will be caught unaware. So the disciples must stay awake, like a homeowner expecting a thief, and like a slave who keeps doing his job while his master is away.
readings: Preterists read the chapter as Jesus' prophecy of the Jewish war. The false messiahs, wars, famines, persecutions, the Roman armies in the holy place, the flight from Judea and the terrible siege all happened within forty years, inside "this generation" (24:34). The darkened sky and the Son of Man on the clouds are the prophets' picture language for God's judgment on a city and the vindication of Jesus. Partial preterists, such as R. T. France and R. C. Sproul, read 24:4–35 this way and then read 24:36–25:46 as Christ's final return. Full preterists, such as J. Stuart Russell (1878), read all of chapters 24–25, the final judgment included, as fulfilled in AD 70; nearly all churches reject that view.
Read as the end of history

Futurists read the chapter as a timeline still to come: the gospel reaches all nations, an Antichrist sets up the abomination in a rebuilt temple, a great tribulation follows, and Christ returns visibly. Dispensational writers apply it especially to Israel in a future seven-year tribulation, after the church has been taken up; historic premillennialists see the church going through the tribulation. Many futurists allow that AD 70 was a first, partial fulfillment.
Read as the pattern of every age

Idealist readers, and many preachers, hear the chapter as a description of the whole time between Jesus' first and second comings: deceivers, wars, persecution and cooling love, alongside the spread of the good news. The fall of Jerusalem is one example of a pattern that keeps recurring, and the point for every generation is the same: do not be fooled, hold out, stay ready.

views.H: Josephus, a Jewish general who went over to the Romans, describes the war of AD 66–70 in detail: rival rebel leaders, men claiming to be prophets, famine in the besieged city, the Temple burned in August 70 and the city pulled down. Historians debate how much of Matthew 24 Jesus himself said, but almost all agree he predicted the Temple's destruction, a charge raised against him at his trial (26:61).
views.C: Matthew follows Mark 13 closely, adding sayings shared with Luke (24:26–28, 37–41, 43–51; Luke 17 and 12). In 1864 Timothée Colani proposed that Mark 13 used a Jewish or Jewish-Christian "little apocalypse." Later scholars, among them Gerd Theissen, suggested that such a source was written when Caligula tried to set up his statue in the Temple in AD 40. Matthew's changes, "your coming," "the end of the age," "on a Sabbath," and the long section on watchfulness, suggest a church after AD 70 dealing with the delay of Jesus' return.
views.L: This is the fifth and last of Matthew's great discourses, closed by the formula that ends each of them (26:1; compare 7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). It mirrors the first: both are given on a mountain, and both end by dividing the sensible from the foolish (7:24–27; 25:1–13). It also forms a pair with chapter 23: the woes against the scribes end in the Temple left desolate (23:38), and the discourse begins with Jesus walking out of it.
views.J: Jesus speaks here as a Jewish prophet in the tradition of Jeremiah, who warned that the Temple would fall (Jeremiah 7; Jeremiah 26), and of Daniel. Jewish apocalypses written after AD 70, such as 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch, wrestle with the same disaster. The rabbis mourned the Temple and blamed baseless hatred among Jews. Later Christians often used this chapter to claim that God had rejected the Jewish people, a reading most churches now repudiate; Jesus grieves for Jerusalem (23:37) and tells his followers to flee, not to rejoice.
views.T: John Chrysostom read 24:4–22 as the Roman war and the rest as Christ's second coming, and many fathers followed a similar two-part reading. Augustine warned against calculating the date (Letter 199, to Hesychius). In the West the passage has long been read in the last weeks of the church year and in Advent, the season that looks to Christ's coming.

deep.b:
The revolt began in AD 66, when the Roman governor Florus took money from the Temple treasury and his troops killed protesters. The rebels stopped the daily sacrifice for the emperor and drove the Roman garrison out. A Syrian army under Cestius Gallus besieged Jerusalem and then, for reasons still debated, withdrew, and was cut up in retreat (Josephus, Jewish War 2.19). Many think this was the moment Christians fled (24:16).

Nero sent Vespasian, who conquered Galilee in 67 (the young commander Josephus surrendered at Jotapata) and then Judea. Inside Jerusalem rival factions under John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and the Zealot Eleazar fought each other, killed priests in the Temple courts and burned the city's grain stores (Jewish War 4–5). After Nero's death and the civil war of 69, Vespasian became emperor and left the siege to his son Titus.

In spring 70 Titus laid siege to the city, and in early summer he surrounded it with a wall (5.12.1–2). Famine grew so severe that Josephus tells of a mother who ate her own child (6.3.4). In August the Temple burned; soldiers set up their standards in the courts and sacrificed to them, hailing Titus as commander (6.6.1). The city was pulled down (7.1.1). Josephus' count of 1,100,000 dead (6.9.3) is surely too high, but the loss was enormous. The Arch of Titus in Rome still shows soldiers carrying the Temple's lampstand.

Most readers mix these. Revelation is read in the same four ways (see the topic page The Four Views).

All three Synoptic Gospels have this talk (Mark 13; Luke 21:5–36). Matthew follows Mark's order closely but adds and changes in ways that show his concerns:

  • The question includes "your coming" and "the completion of the age" (24:3). Mark 13:4 asks when "these things" will be and what sign will show they are about to be accomplished; Matthew names "your coming" and "the end of the age.".
  • "In the whole inhabited world" and "then the end will come" (24:14; compare Mark 13:10).
  • The abomination is named as "spoken of through Daniel the prophet" and stands "in a holy place" (24:15); Luke instead says "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies" (Luke 21:20).
  • "Or on a Sabbath" (24:20).
  • The sign of the Son of Man and the mourning tribes (24:30).
  • The long section on watchfulness (24:37–25:46), most of it shared with Luke 12 and 17, and three parables found only in Matthew or told differently there.

Many scholars think John knew this discourse in some form; Revelation 6 follows its order of disasters closely.

deep.title: Claude's theory: from a building to a person
deep.b: The discourse begins with Jesus walking out of a Temple he has just called deserted (23:38–24:1), and its first words are about stones being pulled down. It ends with a King who says, "you did it for me" (25:40). My suggestion is that Matthew has shaped the whole discourse as a move from the place where God's presence was sought to the persons in whom Christ is now met: the Son of Man in glory and the least of his brothers. The Gospel says this from start to end: Jesus is Immanuel, God with us (1:23); something greater than the Temple is here (12:6); and he promises to be with his followers until the end of the age (28:20), the same phrase the disciples used in 24:3. If this is right, the answer to "when will the Temple fall and the age end?" is partly: the presence the Temple held is now found in Jesus and in those he calls his brothers. This overlaps with the temple theology of scholars such as N. T. Wright and G. K. Beale, but the reading of 24–25 as one arc from building to person is my own proposal.

echoes: Mark 13:1–37; Luke 21:5–36; Luke 17:22–37; Luke 12:39–46; Daniel 7:13–14; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 12:1; Isaiah 13:10; Isaiah 34:4; Zechariah 12:10–14; Genesis 6–7; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:11; 2 Thessalonians 2:1–12; Revelation 1:7; Revelation 6:12–17

settings.to: His disciples, who were pointing out the Temple's buildings as they left it
settings.when: As he walked out of the Temple courts for the last time, during the last week before his death
settings.why: The disciples admired the Temple as the center of Israel's life with God. Jesus answers with a prophet's warning: the building they admire will be pulled down. He had just told the Temple's leaders that their house was left deserted (23:38), so the words carry judgment, not just a forecast.
settings.readers: For Matthew's first readers the Temple was most likely already in ruins. The saying showed that Jesus had foreseen it, and that their faith did not depend on the building.

settings.what: The discourse on the Mount of Olives, Matthew's fifth discourse
settings.to: His disciples, privately, sitting on the Mount of Olives across from the Temple. Mark 13:3 names Peter, James, John and Andrew; Luke 21:5–7 sets a similar talk in the Temple courts.
settings.when: Two days before the Passover (26:2), just after Jesus left the Temple (24:1) and pronounced woes on the scribes and Pharisees (chapter 23)
settings.why: To answer the disciples' question about the Temple and the end. Jesus warns them not to be fooled by false messiahs or panicked by wars, to flee Judea when the sign appears, and above all to stay faithful and ready through a delay of unknown length. Because it is a private talk to followers who would face persecution, it reads less like a timetable for outsiders than like a pastor's warning to his own people.
settings.readers: Matthew's Jewish-Christian readers, most likely after AD 70, could look back on the war Jesus foretold and ask why he had not yet come. The discourse told them that the Temple's fall did not mean the end had come, that the end would come without warning, and that in the meantime they must be faithful slaves, ready bridesmaids, busy servants and merciful neighbors.
views: Most critical scholars date Matthew about AD 80–90 and think the war's memory shaped the wording of 24:15–22.
J. A. T. Robinson and many conservative scholars date Matthew before the war, so that the discourse was read as a prophecy before the event.

settings.what: The parable of the fig tree
settings.to: The disciples on the Mount of Olives
settings.when: In spring, at Passover time, when fig trees put out their leaves
settings.why: To teach that the events he has described can be read as surely as the signs of the season, and to give a firm limit: "this generation." The words were meant to give urgency without anxiety.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers had seen Jerusalem fall within a generation. The parable assured them that Jesus' words had come true and would keep coming true (24:35).

settings.what: The saying of the thief in the night
settings.when: In the discourse on the Mount of Olives. Luke 12:39–40 places the same saying earlier, in a talk to the disciples about not worrying and being ready.
settings.why: To turn the discussion from signs to readiness. Since no one knows the hour, the only safe course is to be ready all the time.
settings.readers: The image spread quickly in the early church (1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 3:3), a sign that Christians remembered it as a key saying of Jesus.

settings.what: The parable of the faithful and the evil slave
settings.to: The disciples. In Luke 12:41–46 the parable answers Peter's question whether the teaching was for the disciples or for everyone.
settings.when: In the discourse on the Mount of Olives
settings.why: To warn those given responsibility over others that the master's delay is not permission to abuse them or to live carelessly. The slave set over the household staff fits leaders of the community.
settings.readers: For a church whose leaders served while the Lord was away, the parable was a warning against bullying and self-indulgence, and a promise to the faithful.

traditions.q: "One is taken along, and one is left behind" (24:40). Is this the rapture of the church?
views: Divided on this verse, though not on the rapture. Dispensationalists teach that Christ will take his church up before the tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), and popular teaching, such as the Left Behind novels, reads 24:40–41 that way. Pre-tribulation teachers such as Tim LaHaye read the verse that way. But many dispensational scholars, including John Walvoord and Louis Barbieri, say Matthew 24 describes the end of the tribulation, and read those "taken" as removed in judgment, like the people of Noah's day, while those left enter Christ's kingdom.

Mostly yes. The Assemblies of God calls the rapture of the church "the blessed hope" and teaches that it may happen at any moment; many Pentecostal preachers use this verse for it. Some Pentecostal groups hold other timings.

Divided. Many American Baptists hold a pre-tribulation rapture. Others, like the Baptist scholar George Eldon Ladd, teach one coming after the tribulation, when the angels gather the chosen (24:29–31). The Baptist Faith and Message does not decide.

No separate rapture. Christ comes once, in glory, after the church has passed through a final trial (Catechism 675–677). The gathering of the chosen (24:31) and being caught up to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17) belong to that one coming.

No separate rapture. The Orthodox expect one visible return of Christ to judge the living and the dead, as the Creed says, and read the verse with the fathers as the separation of the faithful from the unfaithful at that coming.
No. The Augsburg Confession (article 17) teaches that Christ will appear at the end of the world to judge and to raise the dead; there is no hidden coming before it.

No. Christ returns once, visibly, at the last day (Westminster Confession 33). Reformed scholars read the taken and the left as the separation at that coming; some think those taken are taken in judgment.

traditions.q: Do 24:29–34 describe a coming of Christ in AD 70, or his future return?
views: Both levels. The Catechism teaches that Christ's coming in glory is still ahead and will be preceded by a final trial of the church (Catechism 673–677). Many Catholic interpreters read the fall of Jerusalem as a real fulfillment and a sign pointing to the final judgment.
Mostly future, with AD 70 as a first fulfillment. John Chrysostom read 24:4–22 as the Roman war against Jerusalem and the verses after as Christ's second coming (Homilies on Matthew 75–76).

Divided. Calvin held that Christ mixed the fall of Jerusalem with the end of the world. Many Reformed and Presbyterian writers today are partial preterists, reading 24:4–35 as fulfilled in AD 70 and 24:36 onward as the final return (R. C. Sproul, Kenneth Gentry). Full preterism, which says the return has already happened, is rejected by Reformed churches.

Future. Matthew 24 describes the seven-year tribulation, centered on Israel; the abomination is the Antichrist in a rebuilt temple, and "this generation" is the generation alive when these signs begin.

Fulfilled step by step in history. The great suffering was the long persecution of faithful believers in the Middle Ages, and the darkened sun and falling stars (24:29; Revelation 6:12–13) were fulfilled in the Dark Day of 1780 and the great meteor shower of 1833, so Christ's return is near.

Christ's parousia, his "presence," began invisibly in 1914, when he began to rule in heaven. The wars, famines and earthquakes since then make up the sign of that presence, and the end of the present system is close.

title: Lamps, Talents and the Least of These
sum: Jesus ends his last discourse with three pictures of the time of waiting and the judgment that ends it. Ten young women wait with lamps for a groom who is late; the five who brought extra oil go in to the wedding, and the door shuts on the rest. A man going abroad trusts his slaves with huge sums; two put the money to work, and one buries it out of fear and loses everything.

Finally the Son of Man sits on his glorious throne as King and separates all the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Those who fed the hungry, welcomed strangers, clothed the naked and visited the sick and the prisoners are told that they did it for him, and are surprised. Those who did not are sent away into eternal punishment.
readings: Read as warnings to the church

In this reading all three scenes are about Jesus' followers in the time before his return: be ready (the young women), be faithful and productive (the talents), and show mercy, especially to Christ's needy brothers and sisters (the sheep and goats). The church has read the chapter this way in most of its history, and the parables echo the Sermon on the Mount's ending (7:21–27).

Many modern readers hear 25:31–46 as Jesus' statement that every human being will be judged by how they treated the poor, whether or not they knew Christ. On this reading Christ is hidden in every needy person, and mercy is the test of every life. It has shaped much Christian social action, Catholic social teaching and the work of people like Mother Teresa.

Scholars such as Joachim Jeremias argued that the parables first warned Jesus' Jewish hearers about the crisis of his own coming, and that Matthew applied them to the church waiting for his return. On this view the ten young women and the talents first addressed Israel's leaders, who had been given much and were about to be called to account.

views.H: The parables draw on village life: a wedding procession at night, torches that burned out quickly, burying money as the safe way to keep it, bankers who paid interest, mixed flocks of sheep and goats. A talent was a fortune, about twenty years' pay for a worker, so the amounts in the story are deliberately extravagant.
views.C: The ten young women (25:1–13) and the sheep and goats (25:31–46) are found only in Matthew. The talents has a cousin in Luke's minas (Luke 19:11–27), probably from a shared source, though the details differ greatly. Many scholars see Matthew's hand in the final scene's language ("Son of Man," "King," "my Father"), while its core of mercy to the needy is widely thought to go back to Jesus.
views.L: Three scenes build to a climax: a wedding, a business account and a royal court. Each divides people into two groups, and each ends with a verdict. The last scene answers the disciples' question about "your coming" (24:3) with the coming itself. Right after it comes the formula that closes each of Matthew's five discourses (26:1), and the passion begins.
views.J: The works of mercy in 25:35–36 are the Jewish acts of loving-kindness (gemilut chasadim), which the rabbis described as imitating God. Amy-Jill Levine reads the parables as Jewish stories that challenge their hearers rather than as attacks on Judaism. Some Jewish interpreters note that a judgment by deeds, not by belonging to a group, is very close to Jewish teaching.
views.T: The ten young women became a favorite parable of the early church, carved on cathedral doors (as at Magdeburg and Strasbourg) and sung in Bach's cantata Wachet auf (1731). The sheep and goats gave Catholic and Orthodox teaching the corporal works of mercy. Benedict's Rule tells monks to receive every guest as Christ, quoting 25:35 (Rule of Benedict 53).

deep.b:
A Jewish wedding came in two stages. First the couple were betrothed, a binding agreement. Later, often a year after, the groom came to the bride's family home to take her to his own house, where the wedding feast was held, sometimes for a week. He came at night with friends, and young women of the bride's household or village met him with torches and joined the procession. Delays were common while the families finished settling the gifts.

The story does not mention the bride at all (see the variant at 25:1). That keeps the attention on the groom, whom Matthew's readers would recognize as Jesus (9:15), and on the waiting guests.

deep.h: "You did it for me" in church history
deep.b: Early Christians took the scene literally in their care for prisoners and the poor; the pagan writer Lucian mocked Christians for visiting and feeding their imprisoned members. John Chrysostom told his congregation: if you want to honor Christ's body, do not ignore him when he is naked; do not honor him here in church with silk while outside you neglect him cold and naked (Homilies on Matthew 50). Martin of Tours, who cut his cloak in half for a beggar and then dreamed of Christ wearing it, became a famous example. In the twentieth century the passage became central to Catholic social teaching and to many Protestant movements, while scholars such as Ulrich Luz showed that the older church had more often read "the least of these" as needy Christians.

settings.what: The parable of the ten young women (the ten virgins)
settings.to: The disciples on the Mount of Olives, continuing the discourse
settings.when: Two days before the Passover, after the warnings about the unknown hour (24:36–51). Found only in Matthew.
settings.why: To show that readiness cannot be produced at the last minute or borrowed from someone else. The groom's delay tests who has prepared for a long wait. Knowing the hearers were his own disciples makes it a warning to insiders: the foolish young women were invited guests.
settings.readers: For a church that had waited longer than it expected, the story said: the groom is coming, even if late; be prepared for the delay.
views: The usual reading from the fathers on: the groom is Christ, the wedding is the kingdom, the young women are believers.
Jeremias and others think Jesus first told it to warn his own people of the crisis of his ministry, and that Matthew applied it to the return.

settings.to: The disciples on the Mount of Olives. Luke 19:11–27 tells a similar parable of minas near Jericho, to a crowd who thought the kingdom of God was about to appear at once.
settings.when: In the discourse on the Mount of Olives, two days before the Passover
settings.why: To teach that waiting for the master means working with what he has entrusted, not keeping it safe out of fear. The third slave's failure is not losing money but doing nothing, from a false picture of his master.
settings.readers: Matthew's readers were to see themselves as slaves entrusted with the master's property, the good news and the life of the community, during his long absence.
views: The traditional reading: the master returns as judge; faithful use of gifts is rewarded.
A story about an unjust rich man
William Herzog and some others read the master as an exploiting landlord and the third slave as a hero who refuses to cooperate; few interpreters think this fits Matthew's setting.

settings.what: The judgment of the nations (the sheep and the goats)
settings.by: Jesus, speaking of himself as the Son of Man and the King
settings.to: The disciples, at the end of the discourse on the Mount of Olives
settings.when: The last teaching before the passion narrative begins (26:1–2). Found only in Matthew.
settings.why: To show what the coming of the Son of Man will mean: a judgment of all the nations in which mercy to Jesus' "least" brothers is treated as mercy to him. For disciples about to be scattered, persecuted and imprisoned (24:9), it was also a promise that Christ stands with the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner.
settings.readers: Matthew's community, a small group under pressure, heard that the world would be judged by how it treated Christ's needy ones, and that they themselves must show the same mercy.
views: Most modern readers: all people are judged by their mercy to anyone in need.
Many scholars: "my brothers" in Matthew are disciples (12:49–50; 28:10), so the nations are judged by how they received Christ's messengers (10:40–42).
Dispensational writers: the Gentile nations judged at the start of the millennium for how they treated Israel.

traditions.q: Who are "the least" of Jesus' brothers (25:40)?
views: Every person in need. The Catechism says that Christ identifies himself with the poor and that we will be judged by how we respond to their needs, citing this passage (Catechism 544, 1033, 2443–2449).
Every person in need, in whom Christ is met. John Chrysostom told his hearers that whoever honors Christ's body in church must not neglect him naked outside (Homilies on Matthew 50).

Jesus' Jewish brothers. The Scofield Reference Bible and J. Dwight Pentecost read the scene as the judgment of the living nations at Christ's return, judged by how they treated Israel, or the Jewish believers who preach during the tribulation.

Divided. Many evangelical scholars, such as R. T. France, read Jesus' "brothers" as his disciples, so that the nations are judged by how they received his messengers; many others, and much evangelical relief work, read the passage as being about all the poor.

traditions.q: When does the judgment of the sheep and the goats (25:31–46) take place?
views: At the Last Judgment at the end of history, when all the dead are raised and all people are judged. The Church rejects any earthly reign of Christ within history before it (Catechism 676, 1038–1041).
At the last day, when Christ returns to raise the dead and judge everyone, giving eternal life to believers and condemning the ungodly (Augsburg Confession, article 17).
At the one general judgment at Christ's return, the same judgment as Revelation 20:11–15 (Westminster Confession 33.1).

Divided. Historic premillennialists such as George Eldon Ladd hold that Christ returns once, after the tribulation, and reigns for a thousand years before the final judgment; they usually see 25:31–46 as a picture of that general judgment, not a separate judgment of living nations. Other Baptists are amillennial or dispensational. The Baptist Faith and Message does not decide.

At the start of the millennium. When Christ returns after the tribulation he judges the Gentile nations still alive; the "sheep" enter his thousand-year kingdom on earth, and the judgment of the dead at the great white throne comes a thousand years later.
At Christ's return, when the righteous are raised and taken to heaven for the thousand years; the wicked are raised and destroyed at the end of the thousand years.

traditions.q: "Eternal punishment ... eternal life" (25:46). Does the punishment last as long as the life?
views: Yes. The Catechism cites 25:41 and 25:46 and teaches that hell is eternal; its chief punishment is eternal separation from God (Catechism 1034–1035).

Yes, in the church's teaching. Many Orthodox writers, following Isaac the Syrian, describe the fire as God's love felt as torment by those who refuse it, and a few have hoped that all may at last be saved, though the church condemned the teaching that all surely will be (553).
Yes. The wicked "shall be cast into eternal torments, and be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord" (Westminster Confession 33.2).

Divided. Many Anglicans hold the traditional view. John Stott leaned toward final destruction, and the Church of England's report The Mystery of Salvation (1995) described hell as final and total non-being.
No. The word "eternal" describes the result: the wicked are destroyed forever and do not live on in torment.
No. The "eternal punishment" is everlasting cutting-off, death with no hope of resurrection.
